standard_prerequisites.name: Mere propositions, sets and Axiom K
standard_prerequisites.statement: A type is a mere proposition when all its elements are equal; a type X is a set when p = q for all x,y : X and p,q : x = y; Axiom K says p = refl_x for every p : x = x, and the book proves K equivalent to being a set at Theorem 7.2.1.
standard_prerequisites.use: The theorem is stated for a mere relation R implying identity and its conclusion is that X is a set, so both the hypothesis and the equivalence used at source lines 274-278 are level-0 material.

standard_prerequisites.name: Identity types, transport and dependent paths
standard_prerequisites.statement: Transport along p : x = y in a type family, ap of a dependent function, and the dependent path type; the book's Lemma 2.9.6 converts a dependent path in an arrow type into a path between transports.
standard_prerequisites.use: The first author proof at source lines 287-296 is a computation with ap of the dependent function f(x) : R(x,x) -> (x = x) and with the arrow-type dependent path lemma.

standard_prerequisites.name: Total spaces, fibres and the sigma path characterization
standard_prerequisites.statement: For f : A -> B, f is an equivalence as soon as the induced map of total spaces is an equivalence (the book's Theorem 4.7.7), and paths in a sigma type are pairs of a path and a dependent path (the book's Theorem 2.7.2).
standard_prerequisites.use: The second author proof at source lines 299-312 needs exactly these two ingredients to show each f(x,y) is an equivalence.

core_obligations: Show that the two conclusion clauses of the statement are equivalent: X a set makes x = y a mere proposition, and R(x,y) is one by hypothesis, so logical equivalence upgrades to equivalence; conversely an equivalence of x = y with the mere proposition R(x,y) makes X a set (source lines 274-278).

First proof: for x : X and p : x = x, read ap_{f(x)}(p) as a dependent path in the family R(x,x) -> (x = x) and convert it, using the arrow-type dependent path lemma, into trans_p(f(x,x,r)) = f(x,x,trans_p r) for every r : R(x,x) (source lines 287-291).

Collapse the right-hand side by the mere-proposition hypothesis on R(x,x), note that transport in an identity type is concatenation, substitute r := rho(x), and cancel to conclude p = refl_x, hence Axiom K and hence that X is a set (source lines 292-297).
Second proof: reduce the goal that each f(x,y) is an equivalence to contractibility of the total space of R(x,-), using the total-space criterion (source lines 299-304).

Exhibit (x, rho(x)) as centre of contraction of Sm{y:X} R(x,y): given y and H : R(x,y), transport the goal along the sigma path characterization and discharge it by the mere-proposition hypothesis on R(x,y) together with the path f(H) : x = y (source lines 305-312).

proof_roadmap.step: Record that the two clauses of the theorem are equivalent, so that proving either one suffices.
First proof: transport the dependent function f(x) along a loop p, use the arrow-type dependent path lemma and the mere-proposition hypothesis on R(x,x) to force p = refl_x, giving Axiom K.
Second proof: total space of R(x,-) is contractible with centre (x, rho(x)), so each f(x,y) is an equivalence.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is Theorem 7.2.2 at source lines 265-269, and both of the author's proofs are retained (source lines 271-313). The hard step in the first proof is a dependent-path computation: for a reflexive mere relation R implying identity one must read ap_{f(x)}(p) as a dependent path in the family R(x,x) -> (x = x), convert it with the arrow-type dependent path lemma into trans_p(f(x,x,r)) = f(x,x,trans_p r) (source lines 289-291), then use that R(x,x) is a mere proposition to collapse trans_p r to r and cancel to obtain p = refl_x (lines 293-296). The second proof is a different route that needs the total-space criterion for equivalences and the sigma path characterization to show Sm{y:X} R(x,y) contractible with centre (x, rho(x)) (lines 300-312). Neither step is a routine rewrite, and the statement alone supplies neither the transport bookkeeping nor the contractibility witness.
